intent: Expose the three stdio MCP tools and ship the executable with end-to-end protocol verification
Expose the fixed stdio MCP contract and verify the runnable executable

name: ComparisonService
role: Coordinates the existing store reader, repository observer, and drift analyzer for read-only tool operations.
conditions: It returns JSON-compatible views and contains no MCP transport or schema logic.

name: McpServerFactory
role: Registers exactly three schema-validated MCP tools through the synchronous official SDK.
conditions: Every tool requires repository_root and converts application output into MCP text content.

name: FluencyDriftMcpApplication
role: Starts the SDK stdio transport for the executable artifact.
conditions: It performs no custom JSON-RPC framing and keeps the process alive for client requests.

name: Executable protocol test
role: Launches the shaded JAR and verifies initialize, tools/list, and tools/call over stdio.
conditions: It targets the attached -all.jar, so it validates the distributable artifact rather than only compiled classes.

subject: Coverage lifecycle
why: Failsafe runs after package, so JaCoCo reporting and the coverage check execute in verify after all tests.

title: Delegate MCP stdio protocol handling to the official SDK
why: The SDK owns JSON-RPC framing and repository_root schema validation while the application layer remains focused on read-only comparison operations.
alternative: Implement a custom stdin JSON-RPC loop — rejected because it duplicates protocol behavior and validation that the official SDK already provides.

title: Verify the shipped shaded JAR over stdio
why: Failsafe launches the attached executable JAR and checks the public MCP exchange, which proves the packaged entry point and protocol wiring work together.
alternative: Test only in-process classes or a classpath launch — rejected because neither verifies the delivered executable artifact.

title: Promote SDK-owned protocol handling
why: The server boundary is a recurring integration point where SDK ownership keeps protocol concerns separate from product operations.
alternative: Treat the SDK choice as a one-off implementation detail and allow future boundaries to reimplement protocol handling.
